# [Root Cause Of The Odor Generated By Germicidal UV Disinfection With Mobile Units](https://sanuvox.com/en/blog/root-cause-of-the-odor-generated-by-germicidal-uv-disinfection-with-mobile-units/)

The more you disinfect a space with UV light, the less new burned dust you will encounter.

> It was noticed that when the disinfection cycles were repeated several times in the same enclosure, the perceived odor level after each cycle seemed to be diminishing. This was the hint that leads us to focus our attention on the presence of dust particles in the air, what these particles consist of, and how UV can potentially alter them into perceptible odorous compounds.

With each successive UV irradiation, the amount of dust in the air diminishes as more and more of it gets burned off. When keratin from shed skin and hair burns, it is precisely the part that gives it strength and rigidity that gives off the pungent odor. Volatile sulphur-containing compounds can smell like rubber, rotten eggs, or sewage.

> Keratin encloses large amounts of the sulfur-containing amino acid cysteine, required for the disulfide bridges that confer additional strength and rigidity by permanent, thermally stable crosslinking.

Sulphur atoms in cysteine allow for this amino acid to form disulfide, crosslinking bonds. Keratin is over 5% sulphur, and when its bonds with the protein are broken, smaller sulphur-containing compounds become volatile and perceptible by smell.

> The pungent smell of burning hair and rubber is due to the sulfur by-products. The average composition of human hair consists of 45.2 % carbon, 27.9% oxygen, 6.6% hydrogen, 15.1% nitrogen and 5.2% sulphur.

Visible light is not energetic enough to break sulphur bonds in cysteine, but UV light is.

> Proteomic molecules such as keratin and cysteine can be broken up by germicidal UV irradiation but not by visible light, for which the average wavelength is 550 nm, and the maximum photon energy only 217 kJ/mol.

The UV light with the 254 nm wavelength has the photon energy of 470 kJ/mole, which is enough to break many organic chemical bonds.

If a room that is almost too dusty for safe occupancy is irradiated with UV light, it will generate thiol concentrations that still wouldn't make the air unsafe to breathe.

> At maximum ASHRAE acceptable airborne dust loads of 10,000 μg/m³ (0.0044 grain/ft³), concentration of thiol could end up being as high as 200 ppb after UV disinfection.

Thiols (aka mercaptans) are perceptible at 1 ppb, so no one would agree to breathe air with thiol concentration of 200 ppb anyway even though it is still not considered to be a high enough concentration to pose a health risk.

> According to the CSST in Quebec and per OSHA, the safe level for 8 hours of exposure to mercaptans is 500 ppb.

Normand Brais and Benoit Despatis concluded that it is safe to occupy a room with volatile organic compounds from dust burned by UV irradiation.

> Given that the resulting potential concentrations of thiol molecules are negligible when compared to the published acceptable exposure limits, it is safe to enter a room after germicidal UV disinfection has been performed.
